utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. First of all, apologies for the delayed start. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I don't think there are any procedural issues to be raised. One question, could the parties inform me about the time estimates for the present witness, also if you have the scheduling for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I would hope to be done within the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, my initial estimate is two and a half hours, but I do realise that there are scheduling issues, and I'll try to get through as quickly as possible to facilitate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. Then can the witness be escorted into the courtroom, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Corbic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Jordash will now continue his cross-examination. You may proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Corbic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: As we finished off yesterday, your statement, and the map, the chart are now before the Court, so I just want to seek a little clarification of some issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: First of all, could we have the map back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to speak to you first of all -- or ask you about the kind of resources that you had within the Novi Pazar department, and the kind of resources you had overall within the Kraljevo DB centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think I said the exhibit number, D453.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: First of all, are you able to comment or the level of man- or womanpower in the region that you've indicated was covered by the Kraljevo DB centre?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre of DB in Kraljevo consisted of four sections. Section Novi Pazar, section Cacak, section Krusevac, and section Kraljevo. The section of Novi Pazar in the early days, and when I say early days, I mean when the situation was beginning to get more complicated, had seven people working there until the end of 1993. Out of them, five operatives and two administrative employees. At the level of Kraljevo, the Kraljevo centre, I don't know the exact number of staff but roughly -- do you want me to give you a rough figure? Around 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And of them how many were operatives?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the entire centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking, but I'm not sure, around 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in the years from 1991 to 1993 -- let me extend that. From 1991 to 1995, what kind of co-operation did you have with the public security?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The co-operation was very good in terms of sharing information and reports about situations we were not able to deal with independently, mostly crime, smuggling of arms, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What kind of resources did they have within the Kraljevo DB centre territorial area?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a lot more because they had uniformed policemen and they had CID inspectors and just in sheer numbers they were stronger an our section.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me take you to your statement to seek some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could we have D451. I think it's provisionally under seal until we've checked it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are supposed to have checked it by today, isn't it? We hear from you later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 you refer to the Novi Pazar department and it's work aimed at protecting the security and constitutional order, and then you make a comment that: "Especially during 1992 and 1993, the primary aim, prevention of the civil war in Sandzak, was determined based on an ordered of the RDB chief and leadership." What distinction do you make -- looking at the period of 1991 to 1995, what distinctions do you make in terms of the type of work that was being conducted by the Novi Pazar department? Let me simplify that. What was different about 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Serbia developed a multi-party system -- I'm sorry, because I'm mentioning, at least I'm going to mention some people who occupy important positions now. Could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if you are talking about important positions, important positions in what? In state security organs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't hear interpretation. I didn't understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, madam usher, could you assist the witness. Do you now hear me? My question was -- yes. When you are talking about important positions, I asked you important positions in what, would that be in state security or in other positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] State offices in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the parties. The mere fact that people are holding positions now, if it's not in the state security positions, I think falls beyond the scope of the protective measures we've ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: We would agree with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I think I can provide the Chamber with a bit more information. I think the witness is referring to Sulejman Ugljanin and Rasim Ljajic who are both members of the Serbian government, and I think the witness will, as he has in his statement, testify to their activities which might be characterised as terrorist activities during the conflict, and I think that's the witness's concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm again addressing the parties, under those circumstance, would it be wiser to hear this testimony in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I think if the Chamber is minded to do that, that's fine. I don't know that the witness has a -- either a private security interest or what the public interest would be in the public not knowing this witness's views about those people or not having the knowledge that he purports to have about those people. But if the Chamber wishes to proceed cautiously, then we wouldn't object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, could I perhaps add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think perhaps a liberal reading of Your Honours' ruling may incorporate those in the sense that they were state security targets and arguably their associates were sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution, we'll hear this part of the testimony in private session. Yes, we are in private session so perhaps, Mr. Jordash, you repeat your question and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was different about 1992 and 1993 in terms of your work within the Novi Pazar department?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had just begun to say, when the Party of Democratic Action was established, Dr. Sulejman Ugljanin became its leader and Rasim Ljajic was his deputy. In 1991 after Bosnia and Herzegovina seceded from the former Yugoslavia, on the orders of the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say Alija Izetbegovic, Sulejman Ugljanin, with his party, declared an illegal referendum for Sandzak to secede from Serbia. At the same time we were receiving reports that Ugljanin, along with some extremists among his associates, that is to say not all of them, began illegally to arm more extreme-minded people from his party. He sent them for sabotage and terrorist training to Turkey, and all that created an atmosphere of high nationalist tension and incidents. And in order to prevent all that, we worked primarily to prevent a civil war in Serbia, that was our priority, and to protect people and property in Sandzak, which is a part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me pause you there and let me just return you, after you've given the background, to the issue of 1992 and 1993. Did something happen in 1993 to make 1994 and 1995 different to 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do we need to stay in private session?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the orders of the leadership of the service, Jovica Stanisic, that is to say, our priority task was to prevent civil war in Serbia and to provide absolute protection to all the citizens of Sandzak. We are now using terms Bosniak and Muslim to denote one in the same ethnic community, but at that time we called them Muslims. So our priority was to protect Bosniaks and all the citizens of Sandzak and to gather information about the way arming was conducted, how sabotage terrorist groups were being created, and identify the people who had been to training in Turkey. That terrorist training was organised with the help of the Turkish government for the party of Sulejman Ugljanin. When the Operation in May 1993 began, we arrested only their commanders, the commanders of their paramilitary and para-police units. After that operation, towards the end of 1993 and in 1994, when a criminal complaint was filed by the Prosecutor's Office against Sulejman Ugljanin, the security situation improved considerably. The tensions were defused, many terrorists simply fled, left the area, and the situation began to calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what happened to Ugljanin?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ugljanin, when he heard that he was charged, fled to Turkey. He returned in 1997 or 1998, I can't remember, to Serbia and continued to be involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. I think we might be able to go back into an open session now. I want to continue the discussion but, if you can do it without reference to these two then, unless you need to, then we can return to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We then move into open session. So from now on your testimony will be public again. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash. One second. I said please proceed, but I should have waited for Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. For the record we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have please, 1D05100.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you've seen this. It's in Your Honours chart at item 18. It's the proposal for the launching of Operation May 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How long did the operation last?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, how long did it last, the operation? As we can see from the document, second page, was carried out under the name "May 93," if we look at the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It lasted until the moment I was pensioned off. As far as I know, it's still on-going, but I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to page 2 in the English, bottom of page 1 for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want to understand some terms. Can you see the paragraph where it says: "On orders of the Muslim National Council of Sandzak, the Main Staff of Sandzak Defence was formed with the task of co-ordinating all activities aimed at forming illegal paramilitary formations ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "... training them, arming them, et cetera. Also important in this context is the role of the SDA security department and its leaders, especially in terms of sending members of paramilitary formations to Turkey to undergo training there for conducting sabotage operations in the area of the Raska district." What was the Muslim National Council of Sandzak, what did it consist of, what was its objectives?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim National Council of Sandzak was a group of Muslim parties, several Muslim parties that united. They joined forces. Although some of those parties had no more than two or three members. And this was done in order to give them importance. Sulejman Ugljanin, the SDA, and several other Muslim parties that are were active in the territory of Raska set up the Muslim National Council as a united Muslim council that would make decisions on behalf of all the Muslim parties that were there. And that was stipulated in their memorandum as part of the conditions for the special status of Sandzak. The National Council was tasked with co-ordinating all the activities regarding illegal arming, creating paramilitary sabotage groups, sending Muslim youth for training in Turkey, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What percentage -- are you able to say what percentage of the Muslim population of Sandzak did the Muslim National Council represent or purport to represent?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They purported to represent all the Muslims of Sandzak, which was absolutely incorrect. They represented only the extreme segment of the Muslim population because not all Muslims were extremists and not all of them were in favour of the setting up of the Muslim National Council, the militant policies, and the secession of Sandzak from Serbia. In percentage terms, I could say -- or rather, it's very difficult to say. I would say that perhaps 40 per cent of the Muslims were in favour of the Muslim National Council, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you are asking these questions. Of course, the factual basis for the answers is totally unclear. Again, it's common knowledge that political movements often claim to represent a larger group than they may in fact represent. At the same time, what they do represent often if there's no -- if no studies are done is totally unclear. So I do see that you are asking for impressions at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I was -- I hope the next question might allow the Chamber to see something more concrete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's what we are looking forward to. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At paragraph 14 of your statement - we probably don't need to turn to it unless you want to be reminded of it - you note that on the 25th to the 27th of October, 1991, a secret referendum was organised in Sandzak with the question, "Are you for secession of Sandzak from Serbia and the joinder to another republic of the former Yugoslavia," and you note that the results of the referendum were announced through a press conference. Can you recall what the results were?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but approximately 73 or 70 per cent were in favour and the others were against. But I'm not sure about these figures. I'm absolutely not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: On the one hand you had the impression that 40 per cent of the Muslims were in favour of the Muslim National Council, on the other hand you think, although you are not sure, that 70 or 73 per cent of the Muslims within Sandzak answered "yes" to a question suggesting secession from Serbia. Are you able to clarify those two figures?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The referendum on the secession of Sandzak from Serbia was illegal. Actually, it never took part -- it never took place. It was referendum that was not public according to the extremists themselves. They went door to door to ask people to vote. According to what we he know that referendum never took place, however, the results were made public two or three days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, whether it sheds additional light or whether it further confuses is a -- first of all, a political aim to be achieved is not exactly the same as a certain movement representing part of the population. You cannot agree with a party or a movement, but nevertheless support certain aims. So it's all rather confusing. I just want you to know that that's my first impression of this part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that I can bring much more clarity or whether the witness can, but I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was the -- did the political agenda of the Muslim National Council involve secession through politics or secession through violence? What was its intended modus operandi?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intended modus operandi absolutely followed the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina. If you compare -- or rather, I have to go back in order to look at the entire picture. The secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina happened some 20 or perhaps 15 days before this referendum. After that there was this legal referendum and their modus operandi for secession was double-pronged: One was political agenda, and the other was a joint operation by paramilitary and para-police; that's why they armed themselves, that's why they organised training and sent their youth to organised training, and that's why they organised paramilitary forces. According to their political agenda, they had their own security sector in addition to other sectors such as economic, health, and other sectors. They had their own government of sorts and that was all envisaged by the memorandum on the special status of Sandzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were there other political parties within Sandzak who disagreed with the aims, objectives, and means of achieving those aims and objectives of the Muslim National Council?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was the Socialist Party of Serbia comprised of both Serbs and Muslims. They didn't really agree amongst themselves but they supported the state more than anything else. And if you mean Muslim parties, is that what you are asking me about, Muslim parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I was including that in my question.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim parties simply were too scared to separate themselves from the SDA because there was a lot of pressure put on them. They would be boycotted, threatened, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Returning for a moment to Operation May 1993, an operation, as we can see from the document, formed in order to deal in part with the formation of paramilitary formations. Are you able to provide some evidence concerning how serious the problem was? We know from your statement that 10.000 people in Sandzak were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's at, Your Honours, paragraph 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In terms of day-to-day state security business or public security business, how problematic was this in 1991 to 1993 and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the operation started, the security situation in Sandzak was quite volatile. War had started in Bosnia. A lot of Muslims from Sandzak resided in Bosnia. Many Muslims from Sandzak went to Bosnia to fight on the side of the SDA. On the other hand, there were a lot of illegal weapons according to our information. Organised supply of weapons that arrived from Bosnia, or rather, from one part of Bosnia and that were intended for Sandzak did arrive in Sandzak and we received a lot of intelligence about the presence of weapons. Muslims had a habit whenever they had a celebration or a party, they would fire from those weapons, so that fire that was opened disturbed the population to a large extent. In early 1993 we learned about people being sent for sabotage training in Turkey. We also learned about sabotage groups being set up in towns, in Tuti, in Sjenica, and Novi Pazar. We were compelled to undertake very strong measures in order to prevent incidents and ultimately a civil war, and to protect the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What do you mean when you talk about sabotage groups? What were these sabotage groups? What did they consist of?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sabotage groups had three to five members who were all young men who had served in the JNA who had been trained and were prepared to lay mines, to plant explosives and so on and so forth. Their training followed the -- this pattern: First they were trained in rooms where they were shown films. Somebody would explain to them how to make explosives. Their goal was to blow up tunnels, bridges, facilities where people gathered in large numbers. And they were supposed to be armed with an automatic rifle, a hand-grenade, and three knives, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the Chamber wonders to what extent the details of this training is of importance for the determinations. Whether it's groups of three or ten, or whether they had three knives or seven knives. I mean, the testimony is clear to the extent that this witness tells us that it was a problem that they were trained, they were sent to Turkey, prepared for sabotage. Now, it could be that there's any specific reason why we have to know where they were trained, for how long, et cetera, but the Chamber at this moment has not yet, speaking on behalf of all three of us, has not gained the impression that without this knowledge we would be lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I hope very soon that Your Honours will -- I will be able to bring Your Honours to where I'm heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please go there as quickly as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What relationship with these sabotage units have with those who were being sent to train in Turkey? Did you follow my question?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are two different things. Sabotage terrorist groups were set up as part of the SDA and the sabotage and terrorist training of Muslim youth was first followed by the command cadre for their units. The first group consisted of some 50 men, and then the other groups followed. And those were only for the SDA of Novi Pazar, Tuti, and Sjenica, and the group that was trained in Sandzak came from entire Sandzak including Uzice, Novi Pazar, other parts of Sandzak and Montenegro. Those people went to Turkey to be trained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who was, as far as you were aware, training them in Turkey and what kind of training were they receiving before returning to Sandzak?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were partly trained by Turkish officers. And the other parts of the training was conducted by deserters from the JNA, from the former officers of the JNA who were Muslims. The training was aimed at teaching them what the JNA had at its disposal, how to conduct street fighting, how to set up guerilla war, where the JNA's weakest points were, how to fight in the streets in urban areas. And then they also had practical training in shooting, throwing hand-grenades, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Two follow-on questions then we'll return to your statement. First of all, did you in the state security in Novi Pazar or in the Kraljevo DB centre regard it as part of your professional obligations to prevent these extremists travelling to Turkey for training?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our part of the job was also that. But they travelled as civilians, as free citizens with passports. We didn't have any legal right to stop them to prevent their travelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And a similar question in relation to the Muslims who were travelling into Bosnia to fight against the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was the same; however, the intelligence we had was not sufficient for anybody to be prevented from travelling to Bosnia or elsewhere. We didn't have any formal rights to prevent them from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to your statement, and I'm interested in -- just give me a moment. In paragraph 35. Let's go to 36. And I'm interested in a meeting that you refer to where you note that you took part in about two to three, four at the most, meetings with the state security leadership, including Vilotic. We can see a number of people there mentioned. And the meeting also included -- or the meetings included Jovica Stanisic. I want to take you to the meeting where you first saw Jovica Stanisic in his office in Belgrade prior to the submitting of the proposal for operation Operative Action May 1993. Who was at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was attended by Chief Stanisic whom I saw for the first time, as well as the late Vilotic. I believe that one of the attendees was also Ristic, and assistant. And I believe that Deputy Tepavcevic was also there. The objective of the meeting that was attended by myself and the chief of centre was to inform the chief of the service about the situation in Sandzak and the problems connected with that situation. We conveyed to him everything we knew about Sandzak and potential threats that could be felt there. Chief Stanisic listened to us carefully, although my impression was that he had already --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there. Let me take you step by step. Why had the meeting been arranged?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was called up in order to convey information about the threats and dangers threatening Sandzak and also to discuss measures that had to be put in place in order to diffuse the dangerous situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why were you present?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was very familiar with the situation in Sandzak, and that's why the chief of Kraljevo asked me to come with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How long did the meeting last?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An hour, an hour and a half, perhaps two.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what precisely was discussed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, could you please come to your point. I checked on the transcript, the last five minutes there was nothing of substance which added to what we have already in the statement. Who were present, what was done during these meetings, et cetera. Now, of course, we have additional information that we know that it lasted for one hour or one hour and a half. If it would have been two and a half hours, it would not have been really different for this Chamber. Could you please come to relevant important matters in addition to what is already in the statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In your statement, Mr. Witness, you mention that there was -- and I quote: "There was talk about the potential need, i.e., possibility to establish a unit within the MUP RDB Serbia which would be trained for prevention of activities of terroristic groups." Are you able to elaborate on that conversation, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That conversation took place at the following meeting in the office of the chief of the service. In view of the difficulties we encountered and the problems involving arms and sabotage units as well as the disarming of people, that was not a request. That was a conversation about a unit that would be set up in order to prevent the actions of terrorist and sabotage groups. That would also undertake large scale disarming. There were a lot of weapons and we were not in a position, we did not have enough capabilities to counter all that. That was just the conversation, nothing came out of that. We just discussed potential solutions. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And as far as you can tell, when was that meeting, please? What month and what year?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1993, the second half of 1993. I can't remember now exactly. I believe it was the second half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And from your professional perspective, how useful would an anti-terrorist unit have been in Sandzak in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from my professional perspective, if that unit had been in place in 1992, 1993, and 1994, it would have facilitated our work a great deal. It would have been easier for us to deal with the situation and calm it down, which eventually only happened in 1995, but that unit would have been really very useful to Sandzak because we had all sorts of situations to deal with that were very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever have an anti-terrorist unit come into Sandzak between 1991 and 1995 to assist in any way, an anti-terrorist unit belonging to the DB?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never had that. Nobody ever came apart from the police. The public security department had some units of its own, some detachments, but we never had such a unit. Never existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to Operation May 1993, what kinds of weapons and what kind of numbers were seized during that operation between 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were mostly infantry weapons, rifles, semi-automatic and automatic rifles, machine-guns and submachine-guns, grenades, pistols, one anti-aircraft machine-gun was seized, Zolja hand-held rocket-launchers, mines and explosives, communication devices, and we even seized some chemicals that we later sent for analysis and it turned out they were poisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were there any international observers or representatives of the international community who had any oversight of this operation at any stage?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a OSCE mission at the time in Novi Pazar because the Muslim National Council, that is to say the SDA, kept talking all the time about how Muslim were threatened, how they can't exercise their rights, et cetera, et cetera. This operation in 1993 when we disarmed the security department of Sulejman Ugljanin, seizing a large amount of weapons, including, I remember this very well, three automatic weapons, MGV, produced in Slovenia that were banned by international conventions. In agreement with our chief and the chief of state security, we invited this mission, showed them the weapons, and their comment was that it was classic terrorism. I'm telling you this because I was there. They left Novi Pazar a few days later and never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, between 1991 and 1995, did anyone make any complaints to any Serbian authority concerning your behaviour in relation to Muslim detainees?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, the interpretation I got was Muslim detainees. We never had that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. There may be some suggestions that you were -- acted in a brutal fashion towards certain Muslims who were detained for police interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has just answered that question. He said that this they never had any Muslim detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think Mr. Jordash described it in a bit of a different way. He is entitled to seek verification of the previous answer. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you follow my question. I think the -- there's going to be some suggestions that you were responsible for mistreating Muslims during the course of your professional work. Could you give a response to that? I won't delve into the specifics, I'll leave that to the Prosecution, but if you would like to just respond to that before we finish -- before I finish.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody in any state agency complained about their treatment by the state security section of Novi Pazar. Not that I know of at least, nor were there any proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Have you subsequently been charged with any alleged offences during the course -- committed allegedly during 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've got no further questions, thank you, Mr. Corbic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Perhaps one question in relation to the last two questions, Mr. Corbic. You said that there were no Muslim detainees, at the same time when the question was put to you again, you said there were no complaints in relation to what was again described by Mr. Jordash as Muslim detainees. Could you clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a distinction in my mind. A detainee is somebody who is arrested, kept in prison, et cetera; whereas, people who are brought in, remanded in custody, or just brought in for an interview is something different, at least in my book, than a detainee. Detainee to me means that somebody is sitting in prison, in detention. That's perhaps the explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And both categories are deprived of their liberty, the one perhaps during a short period of time taken into a police station, the other one to end up in a more permanent detention situation; is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We never detained anyone for long. People would be brought in for an interview. Sometimes through a summons, sometimes without a summons because we would, for instance, get a report that somebody was in illegal possession of a weapon and then we would bring that person in. That's the distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One other additional question before I give an opportunities to Mr. Bakrac to cross-examine you. You were asked by Mr. Jordash about the arms that were seized -- well, we already find in your statement, paragraph 40, that these were infantry weapons, explosives, bombs, anti-aircraft machine-guns, Zolja and pistols. So you repeated that testimony. But you added two categories. One was chemicals, and you said it was poison; second, what you refer to as MGV. Could you tell us what the poison was? What poison was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were two small bottles that we sent for analysis because we were not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I didn't ask you whether the poison was in bottles or in boxes or in anything else. What kind of poison was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not get feedback.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say it was poison but without any detail as what kind of poison, whether it would be good for rats or for human beings or we don't know? From your body language, I understand that you have no knowledge. Then you referred in addition to what we find already in your statement to an illegal weapon, MGV. Could you tell us -- I've got no idea what MGV stands for, could you explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] MGV is a Slovene weapon manufactured in Slovenia. An automatic rifle that has a drum at the top, uses small calibre ammunition, 22 millimetres which is small calibre ammunition, prohibited by the Vienna Convention, and that's what we found in the security section of the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What -- you described it as an automatic rifle with a drum, the calibre of the ammunition, and you then say it's prohibited by the Vienna Convention. What distinguishes this weapon from other automatic rifles so that it is prohibited by the Vienna Convention? What's so special about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ammunition that it uses makes it prohibited. It's a small round that is considered to be inhumane, if, of course, any round can be considered humane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's rather the ammunition than the weapon that is illegal; is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That weapon can use only that ammunition, and it's made for that ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I must say I'm unfamiliar with the matter, but thank you for that answer. Mr. Bakrac, any -- yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Before -- sorry, Mr. Bakrac. I've been reliably informed by the B/C/S speakers in the Defence that there is a distinction between prisoners and detainees, and there's a distinction -- there's a distinction in the Croatian word and the Serbian word, and I think that may well have been at the base of the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the witness explained himself on why he said at one moment that there were no Muslim detainees and at another moment he explained it sufficiently and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I clearly accept -- I gladly accept that it may have been caused by language issues. Mr. Bakrac, we are about to have a break, but I would first like to inquire with you how much time you would need, whether you have any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have questions for this witness, two or three questions, and one video that lasts two or three minutes. I hope it won't take more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we had -- we started ten minutes late, of course I am aware that the accused were waiting already in the courtroom. Mr. Jordash, I'm addressing you, knowing the reliability of the estimates of Mr. Bakrac, would we -- would you prefer to hear this testimony before the break in the next ten minutes or would you prefer to have a break first?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think both Mr. Bakrac and Mr. Stanisic would like a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have a break. No problem. We take a break and resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I again have to apologise. Sometimes, as you may have experienced as well, sometimes the breaks require even more of your attention than the full attention already given when being in court. Mr. Bakrac, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Corbic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Bakrac is counsel for Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Corbic. I've already been introduced to you and I have a few questions. If I understood well your written statement and your evidence, you were responsible for the territory of Sandzak with an 80 per cent Muslim and 20 per cent Serb population; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The territory of Sandzak is on the territory of Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you had lot operational information that --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but I have to specify the term "Sandzak." Sandzak includes Novi Pazar, Sjenica, and Tutin, but also Priboj, Prijepolje, Novo Varos. Even in part of Montenegro the term "Sandzak" applies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, perhaps I was not precise enough but I was trying to save time. My mistake. What I mean, the territory under your responsibility falls under the territory of Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, you had a lot of operational information that a large number of Muslims, or in other words, Bosniaks, who were nationals of Serbia were going to Bosnia and fighting on the side of the Green Berets, that is to say, the Muslim Army?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether in the town of Novi Pazar, in its hotels and restaurants, there were seeing-off ceremonies and celebrations for these people who were going to fight in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall those send-offs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understood your evidence correctly, you didn't take any steps against these people because they were going as volunteers. As nationals of Serbia, they crossed the border and they went as volunteers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had no legal requirements met to apply any measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the same way, did Serbs go as volunteers to Bosnia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the area of Sandzak, not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Serbs went from any other area of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I read in the press, yes, I do know about that, but not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your opinion, if these Serbs were also going as volunteers, would you be able to arrest them or take them into custody?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. There would be no legal grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Corbic. You said in your evidence that in various operations, especially Operation May 1993, you seized a large quantity of weapon. Can you give us an approximation of the amount?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a huge quantity, 2, perhaps 2 and a half thousand rifles, plus I don't know how many grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did this operation target only Muslims or did it apply to the entire population?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That operation covered all persons in illegal possession of weapons. There were cases when we prosecuted certain Serbs after we seized weapons from them. People who were involved in arms smuggling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you remember if all the people, and I'm now especially interested in Muslims, were prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The only ones prosecuted were those about whom we had firm evidence that they had procured weapons for the purpose of getting involved in a violent secession of that territory. In all other cases, we would seize weapons, file reports, and release them, and that was done in agreement with the president of the supreme court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that the intention was to calm down the situation in that area, to pacify it, to prevent the security risks intentions from getting worse, or was there another intention?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are absolutely right. Our purpose was to prevent war, to protect all people and property, and to calm the situation in Sandzak down to enable people to live and work normally. And I think that was fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you remember if there was perhaps a legal action by the courts and the police wherein citizens were invited to hand-over weapons in their illegal possession voluntarily without any consequences for them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two such drives, and I believe the turn-out of citizens was the highest in that area of the Raska district. Such weapons would then be legalised and no sanctions were applied against those who turned over their weapons in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was asking. Those weapons that could be legalised were legalised, the weapons that could not be legalised were --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Turned over to the competent authorities with no consequences for the person whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I have only one question remaining, witness, concerning a video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And while we are waiting, it's 2D879 in e-court. There is a transcript. The video footage was recorded by a foreign TV crew, and the booths have received the transcript. 2D879.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Corbic, could you please watch this video and then we'll discuss it very briefly. I just want to know if you are familiar with some of its details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: "Reporter: The Yugoslav wars have introduced a new and fearful phrase to the world's lexicon: 'Ethnic cleansing.' And the terror that is ethnic cleansing has created masses of refugees in every state and every region of what once was Yugoslavia. "Some days the more you get to know about the former Yugoslavia, the more confused you get."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's stop for a second. Have you provided a transcript to the transcriber as well so that we -- apparently you have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our Case Manager provided copies to the usher. I don't know how many copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because the text may be relevant, I see that the transcriber has received a copy by now. Unfortunately, transcription is not made by a team of two but just by one transcriber, so the solution which helps out the interpreters will not help out our transcriber. Let's see to what extent we can perhaps with this text have the transcript be completed after we've seen the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the transcript is also in e-court which diminishes the importance of having it transcribed now and that is of -- an accurate transcript is of utmost important for the proceedings, but here we have a -- we have a remedy in the transcript being filed. Let's proceed. Could we restart, looking at the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: "Anchor: The Yugoslav wars have introduced a new and fearful phrase to the world's lexicon: 'Ethnic cleansing.' And the terror that is ethnic cleansing has created masses of refugees in every state and every region of what once was Yugoslavia. "Some days the more you get to know about the former Yugoslavia, the more confused you get. This will be one of those days. Four hundred and fifty kilometres from Sarajevo inside Serbia, sort of in the middle of nowhere, in a place called Rtanj. We had heard some international observers refer to Rtanj as a place where Serbs warehoused Muslim refugees. Some even called it a prison camp. What we found was something pretty different "If Rtanj is a prison camp, it's not like any prison camp you've read about in the history books. Here children fashion makeshift skis and play carefree. These children are Muslims from Bosnia. They've come here with their mothers to escape the violence of their homeland, and these Muslims say they have found refuge in orthodox Serbia. Silvana Sekic is from Sarajevo. She has been in Serbia with her two children for nearly a year. "Silvana Sekic: The most important thing to realise is that we fight each other in Bosnia but here we all live together so peacefully and so calmly. We eat together, we sleep together, we play together. We have absolutely no problems with each other. We feel like a family here. "Anchor: Nina Brajovic has lived here with her two children for seven months. "Nina Brajovic: We have no problems here at all. Our children play together, our children are given gifts by the Serbs here, and we have absolutely no -- no problem. We've never been harassed, our children felt very welcome. "Anchor: Serbs insist the world's image of them as rapists and ethnic cleansers is especially hurtful given their record in places like Rtanj. After all, the Serbs say, while Muslim women and children are being cared for here, their husbands, fathers, and brothers may very well be fighting and killing Serbs on the battle-fields of Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Corbic, let me ask you first, if this video that we've shown you reflects the situation as you saw it in Sandzak?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I asked you to stop for a second because the French translation was -- had not yet been finished. It has now, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Corbic, you've given me your answer too quickly, perhaps. I was going to ask, the families of all the Muslims, Bosniaks, who stayed in Sandzak, although their fathers and husbands and brothers went to fight elsewhere, they were safe, nobody touched them and the police protected them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody touched them. The police protected everyone and they suffered no consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And my last question, because we've heard evidence here concerning Muslim refugees from Bosnia, that referred to inhumane treatment. Apart from this place Rtanj that we've seen in the video, do you know if there were more refugee camps in Serbia where Muslims were admitted, accommodated with protection of their safety, provision of food, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in my territory. I heard about the territory of Serbia, that there were such camps, but I don't know any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So there were no such camps on your territory, but you cared for the safety of all those Muslim families whose brothers, husbands, fathers went elsewhere to fight?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Corbic. Your Honours, those were all my questions. I hope I did not go beyond my time assessment, although I did a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, this video you've just shown dates from when?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not tender the video-clip into evidence because it will be just one part of the entire material that will be subject of our request to be added to our 65 ter list together with some other witnesses including the author of all those materials that we will eventually tender as a whole. I believe that that will take place very soon. We will very soon request -- file a request for our 65 ter list of evidence and witnesses to be supplemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Bakrac, video was played in court, so therefore for anyone wanting to follow the proceedings or any Appeals Chamber which would eventually have to look at these proceedings, I think it should be at least MFI'd. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is what I was going to suggest, and the Prosecution would not object to an oral application to add it to the 65 ter list this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although Mr. Bakrac is cross-examining, so the material he is using doesn't need to be added to the 65 ter list, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the request for adding it to the -- the request which was not made orally, there's no need to make such a request; and second, I think it would be good to have it at least MFI'd. We have now the full text at my -- my half. Transcriber who --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- who managed to get the whole of the spoken text in the transcript, so people do not have to find it elsewhere. Mr. Bakrac, what about having it MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my understanding was along the lines of your explanation, and that was the -- there was no need for an oral application. I wanted the document to be MFI'd, and then when we have all the materials in place, that MFI number could be removed. At the moment, I would like to tender the video-clip under an MFI number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number under which this video and related transcript is marked for identification would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be D454.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And has the status of marked for identification. Mr. Bakrac, you apparently were referring several times to the video when you said that the husbands, fathers, and brothers were sent for fighting and killing, maybe killing Serbs on the battle-fields. Just in order to be very accurate, the video doesn't say that they were, but it reads literally: "After all, Serbs say while Muslim women and children are being cared for, their husbands," et cetera. So that is a quote from what Serbs say, and it's not presented as a fact but rather as a quote from what Serbs are saying. I just wanted to have that accurate on the record. Unless you disagree with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I completely agree with you. I apologise if I have created confusion. My intention was to use this witness in order to check whether the situation was similar in the territory of Sandzak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Corbic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Farr. Mr. Farr is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I'd like to start by asking you a little bit about the relationship between public security and state security. During your evidence in chief, you've already said that the co-operation between public security and state security was good. I just want to go into a bit more detail. In paragraph 36 of your statement you describe a meeting you had with Jovica Stanisic related to Operation May 93. You say that Stanisic instructed you to "intensify co-operation with other departments and the DB centres including the RJB." First of all, the reference to the RJB is public security; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you recall precisely what Jovica Stanisic said to you when telling you to intensify your co-operation with public security?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that conversation. The public security sector is independent from the state security sector. The public security sector has its tasks which is the protection of the constitutional order, whether the public security sector is concerned with policing, public order, traffic and so on and so forth. Which means that our duties and tasks do not overlap. As for the intensification of our co-operation, this should have related to the protection of public law and order, reducing the rate of crime, and so on and so forth. From the beginning of our Operation May 1993, according to the statistical data, we can see that the rate of crime was reduced, the number of incidents was reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: My question was what precisely Jovica Stanisic said to you when he told you to intensify your co-operation with public security at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please switch off his mike. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I've answered. We were supposed to talk to those people more often and to prevent inter-ethnic conflicts, to prevent crimes, to exchange information, to exchange intelligence, that we should provide them with everything that we were able to provide them. We couldn't give them everything because we were state security and they were public security. All that was aimed at increasing the safety of citizens and their property.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So it sounds to me that essentially there was a shared task: State security did what it was best at and public security did what it was best at; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Now, at the time of that meeting the head of public security of Serbia was Radovan Stojicic, Badza, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So your instruction from Jovica Stanisic was essentially an instruction or an order that the people who worked for him should intensify their co-operation with the people who worked for Badza; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question. Could you please repeat, perhaps rephrase. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Certainly. Stanisic's instruction was that essentially the state security, that is people working for Jovica Stanisic, should co-operate more intensely with public security, that is people working for Radovan Stojicic; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exactly understand what you mean when you say "his men." Those were not Stojicic's men, they were employees of the public security sector and Stanisic's men were he employees of the state security sector. I don't know what Stojicic told them, but I know what my chief told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. And you agree that the people in public security ultimately reported to Radovan Stojicic, Badza? I think that was my point.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic's instruction to you to intensify your co-operation with public security was then reinforced when you received his written decision dated 13 September 1993, regarding Operation May 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are referring to the situation after the start of May 1993 operation; right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: We should probably look at the document for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we could have 1D5100. The middle of page 4 in the English and the bottom of page 4 in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So the point I wanted to direct your attention to was the portion that says: "The need for the RDB or state security department of the MUP and the RJB or public security department of the MUP to take energetic measures and actions." My question is, these words in Stanisic's decision reinforced his oral instruction to you to co-operate with public security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. I'd now like to ask a few more questions about the meetings that you had with Jovica Stanisic outlined in paragraph 36 of your statement. In that paragraph you first talk about a meeting you had with Mr. Stanisic and others in Belgrade in 1993. You said that you went to brief Jovica Stanisic and then you go on to say: "Chief Stanisic listens to me carefully but from his speech I realised that he had already had some findings regarding the events in the field." It's fair to say in your experience Jovica Stanisic was a well informed leader; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my experience, I am afraid I don't have much experience with the top leaders, but as far as the area that I covered, I can say from experience that he was indeed well informed. I don't know whether he was as well informed about the rest of the situation. I don't know. I apologise, he was informed, he was well informed because he relied on the information that we had provided him with before the meeting. I would say that he was well prepared for meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Right. So he had carefully reviewed the information that you had provided to him as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You also describe how he took a personal interest in events in your area and told you that you could count on assistance from RDB headquarters. Specifically you said: "He particularly of emphasised that if it deems to be necessary, we could count on assistance of the RDB headquarters including assistance in manpower and equipment." It's fair to say that in your experience, Mr. Stanisic was an active and involved leader of state security; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only talk about Sandzak. As far as Sandzak is concerned, I would absolutely agree with you. The assistance he provided came in the form of instructions as well as equipment including cars and other things that were necessary, so, yes, I would agree with that. I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. And just to clarify, I'll always only be asking you about things you know about. I'm never going to ask you based on someone else's experience. We are only interested in what you can say from your own experience. At that meeting Mr. Stanisic also gave you an instruction to intensify your co-operation with public security, as we've already discussed. It's fair to say that in your experience Jovica Stanisic was a leader who could work with people outside of state security to get a job done; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 36 after you discuss the meeting in Belgrade you go on to talk about Mr. Stanisic's visit to Novi Pazar. You said he came: "To obtain direct knowledge about the results of previous work of OA May 1993." In your experience, Jovica Stanisic was a leader who took steps to keep himself personally informed about the activities and results of the people who worked for him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that Chief Stanisic, together with the leadership and operatives of Kraljevo and Novi Pazar, prevented the break-out of war in Sandzak. In view of the security situation that prevailed in Sandzak, after the departure of particular leaders of some extremist parties, the situation greatly improved. The arrival of Jovica Stanisic was aimed at finding out whether the situation had indeed improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So he was not content to rely just on the reporting. He wanted to verify for himself in the field what had happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have just said that you will only ask me about the things that I know firsthand, and I will only speak about Sandzak and I will say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, correct me if I'm wrong, but in fact you were three levels down from Mr. Stanisic in the DB hierarchy but he still met with you, listens to you, knew what you were working on, and knew how it was going; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was because of the security situation in the territory of Sandzak, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In paragraph 26 of your statement you say that your "activities were applied pursuant to RDB orders from Belgrade and the head of the RDB Jovica Stanisic." It's fair to say that Jovica Stanisic was aware of your tasks, your methods, and your results when it came to fighting Muslim extremism; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that he knew everything but he was well informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So he was at least generally familiar with your tasks, your methods, and your results?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We briefed him; he read our notes and reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In paragraph 36 of your statement, as far as I can tell you describe two to four meetings at which Jovica Stanisic was personally present and at which you briefed him about Operation May 1993; is that correct? Just yes or no if you can.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly whether there were three or four, hard to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: What kind of information did you provide to Jovica Stanisic during these meetings?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information about the current situation, about what was going on in the territory of Sandzak. The security problems, our main training and so on and so forth. Basically we told him about the grave situation in Sandzak, about people's fear of a possible war.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: What kind of questions did he ask you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His questions were about the veracity of our information, whether the information that we provided him with had been verified, and so on and so forth. They were the usual professional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did he offer any suggestions or recommendations as to how you do your work?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His recommendations and suggestions were not to create a situation, not to compound a situation even further, to try and pacify the situation, to try and prevent incidents, possible war conflicts. That we should resort to repression only if we had to. That we shouldn't be the ones to add fuel to the fire in Sandzak. All he wanted was peace and security and we shared those thoughts with him. He wanted what all of us wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. Before we move on to discussing your work against Muslim extremism, I have a couple of questions about DB administrative procedures that I think you might be able to help with.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And if we could have on the screen 65 ter 6280. I don't think this should be broadcast. This is a document that purports to be a list of per diems paid to five people, including one named Vlado Corbic. Vladimir Corbic, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So, sir, is it correct that you were sometimes paid per diems in connection with your work for the DB?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I worked around the clock, 24-hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So under what conditions would you be -- or what situations would you be paid a per diem?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we worked extended ours and when our engagement was bigger, more extensive, longer. When our engagement went beyond the roles of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did it relate only to working time or did it also relate to the place where you were working. In other words, would you receive a per diem when you worked outside your normal duty post?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Not actually outside the working post, but outside our place of residence and also when we worked extended hours. So that applied to both those situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on the stamp and signature, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct this that this document is signed by Milan Prodanic, the chief of the 8th Administration?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with his signature, but if the name on the signature is Milan Prodanic, then I suppose it's okay. I'm not familiar with his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us anything about the small Roman numeral II that appears inside the seal or stamp?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this as a Prosecution exhibit under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a closer look at the stamp so that we know exactly what you are asking about. Oh, under the --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Underneath the design of the centre of the seal there's a small Roman numeral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, just above where the word "Beograd" gives an R.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just an objection in terms of relevance. I'm not sure what the relevance is and what the witness's answers have added to the evidence. Or to clarification of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Well, it corroborates his evidence that he received per diem payments under the circumstances that he described.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I don't think there's any dispute about that, so I'm not sure we need corroboration of it. I think there's a different purpose to this and it relates to what my learned friend asked about the number 2, and I've no idea what that is about. I don't think the Court would know what that's about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I would like to add to that that you should allow the witness to look at the stamp more closely because it says the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, nothing else. So this, as Mr. Jordash has suggested, could be Roman II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, Mr. Jordash says that there's no dispute about the witness receiving per diems. Despite this, you want to tender it. Do you want to have in evidence the Roman II?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to tell the Court what we think that that may be. We think -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- first of all, let's ask the witness, do you understand and speak English, Mr. Corbic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you please take your earphones off. Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution believes that that may relate to the 2nd Administration of the DB. If the witness was receiving a payment from the 2nd Administration of the DB, that could go to bias.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I think that should be put directly to the witness so he can deal with it, then we might have clarification of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness says he doesn't know what the Roman II stands for. I do understand that Mr. Farr wants to reserve his position as to perhaps seek further evidence, whether what he says is the meaning of this and for that reason to have this in evidence so as that it's there. But I think it would be fair, Mr. Farr, that you also put to the witness apart from whether he knows anything about stamps, whether he knows anything about the origin of the payment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: My objection is then withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the number of this document would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be P3030.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. No need to have it on this -- it was not shown to the public. We do not know, of course, about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Given that the witness is a former member of the DB, it seems at least possible that the others are as well, and if that is indeed Milan Prodanic's [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or perhaps still are. So it -- its admitted under seal. Then, Mr. Farr, you'll put your next question to the witness, who is invited to have his earphones on again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, as far as you know, did you ever receive a per diem payment from the 2nd Administration of the DB?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we please now have 65 ter 6279 on the screen. And again not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, are you going to further pursue the matter you asked the witness about?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, then I would like to put an additional question. Who did pay the per diems to you, Mr. Corbic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The treasurer from Kraljevo centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did he tell you from what budget these per diems were paid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I then understand that that what budget was burdened with the per diems, you do not know exactly?
