utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I suppose it's from the budget of the service. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you don't have any details about which section of the service would pay for the per diems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know it was the 8th Administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because whenever we write requests and travel orders and when we fill in forms to get our expenses compensated for field missions, for instance, we write to the 8th Administration, the section in Kraljevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether they would then -- whether it would then be the 8th Administration which would have the burden of paying you or whether it was any other section, do you have any precise information about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was only the 8th Administration. I don't know about any others. I'm sure it's only the 8th Administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, this document is entitled "List of Payroll Documents to Be Entered." And it is dated 4 December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And if we could please zoom in on the name at number 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name at number 14 as your name, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And if we could scroll to the right for the amount.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you know why you received a per diem of 75 million dinars on 4 December 1993?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the top, please? I don't know what this is. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you -- I know there was a lot of inflation at that time. Do you know for how many days a per diem of 75 million dinars would have been in December of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One or two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: One or two days, yes. This was a period when you were heavily involved in anti-terrorist activities, I think you told us, and also the period in which you would have liked to have had the help of a special anti-terrorist unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been nice if it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And especially at this time in December of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. December, January 1993, also 1994 when the tensions were high.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Now, during your testimony today you said of the unit that we never had that, that it never existed. Can we agree that all you can say is that you never learned of the existence of such a unit and that such a unit never came to Sandzak; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can say that, although if such a unit had been there because of the tensions and because of the weapons involved, et cetera, we would have probably asked for their assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we please have -- sorry, can we please zoom in on lines number 25 and 26 on this document at the bottom. Both across the whole page, yeah, like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, lines 25 and 26 of this document say daily allowances for ATD units. Line 25 is for approximately 12 billion dinars and line 26 is for approximately 121 billion dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we could scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: We could see at line 3 that the Belgrade CRDB received only about 4.4 billion dinars at the same time. Are you aware of any reason that something that is designated as an anti-terrorist unit would be receiving more than 130 billion dinars, while the Belgrade CRDB received less than 5 billion?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I see this document for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And you maintain your evidence that you are not aware of the existence of an anti-terrorist unit within the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I tender this document as a Prosecution exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P3031 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3031 is admitted under seal. Mr. Farr, your questions have triggered my attention to numbers above the word "Beograd." Witness, could you tell us on the stamp on the document we last saw, we see CCCX approximately at the same place where you earlier were asked about a Roman II. Do you know what it stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, if it is Roman as well, then it should be 310. I'm just wondering what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Presumably not the 310th Administration, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Presumably not, I would agree with that. Which leaves the question open what it does mean. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, if we can now turn to the purpose of your work fighting Muslim extremism in the Novi Pazar DB department. In paragraph 27 of your statement you say: "The primary goal of our work was not to obtain information on war conflict and crimes." I think this is relatively clear from your evidence already, but I want to make sure that I understand you. The two primary goals of your work were preserving the territorial integrity and constitutional order of Serbia, and the second was to prevent illegal arming; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Any information you gathered about war crimes was just something you happened to learn in the course of pursuing these other goals; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In your statement you say that the purpose of your work was to prevent the illegal secession of Sandzak from Serbia. You also mentioned the principle of territorial integrity set out in the SFRY constitution. It is correct that in your view the possible secession of Sandzak was illegal precisely because it violated that principle of territorial integrity?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it's also so under the constitution. That is considered to be anti-constitutional activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And this view was shared by your DB colleagues, including Jovica Stanisic, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And it was precisely because this potential secession was illegal that the DB had a duty to prevent it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters cannot hear the witness well when the microphone of the counsel is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Based on that same principle of territorial integrity, did you consider the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia from the SFRY to be illegal as well?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina was mono-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And in your view illegal?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not approved by all the peoples who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Was it illegal?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Was that view shared by your DB colleagues?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Does the same apply to Croatia, you also thought that the secession of Croatia was illegal?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, we were not thinking about that. What was done was done. That was outside our powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: At one point in your statement you referred to Alija Izetbegovic's extremism. Why do you consider Alija Izetbegovic an extremist?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in agreement with the party leader in Sandzak, he was negotiating the arming of people, the distribution of arms. It was through him that training was organised in Turkey, and it was thanks to him and with the help of one person in Vienna that the distribution of arms was financed. All aimed at causing -- starting a war in the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you consider Radovan Karadzic to be an extremist?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, a similar question was put in relation to Izetbegovic and then you had no difficulty in understanding the question. The question is exactly the same but now in relation to Mr. Karadzic. So therefore understanding the question -- if you say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had extremist views of his own which I did not approve.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: What about Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of my republic, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you consider him an extremist?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered him as the president of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, therefore, you didn't consider whether he was right or wrong by the same standards that you applied to other people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same standards applied to everyone, but I don't understand why you're asking me about the man who was the president of my country, whether he was an extremist or not. I'm not able to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, to the extent you wanted to draw our attention that possibly this witness may have been selective in who he called an extremist or what kind of activity he called extremist activity, you have done that. If there is any other purpose for your questions, then please make clear to the Chamber what you are actually seeking as evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, I'd now like to turn to your methods of work in inviting Muslim extremism. In paragraph 32 of your statement, you say that your work was complicated by the fact that: "A substantial number of Muslims boycotted the state organs including organs of the MUP and DB Serbia." You say that this created difficulties in your data gathering. Is it correct that some Muslims would have viewed talking to the DB as a betrayal of their own people?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And in addition to that, they would have been reluctant to tell you anything that could have led to criminal liability for themselves, their friends, or their family; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not always. When they realised how honestly the service was working and what we want, that was already the end of 1993 and 1994, our work became much more efficient and we didn't have to put in so much effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You've already said that as a practical matter, you couldn't investigate war crimes committed by Muslims because the Muslims simply wouldn't tell you about them. I assume that they were no more eager to tell you about their secret - and as you say - illegal arming, training, and plans for secession?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two different types of sources are involved. A Muslim from Sandzak could not speak about war crimes in Bosnia. We could only get that information from a Muslim coming from Bosnia to Sandzak. We invited them for interviews but they were reluctant to talk. Still, if we had some initial information we would write up a report to Kraljevo and Kraljevo would send it on to other centres that could check what was going on, if it was going on; whereas, getting information from Muslims in Sandzak it was a problem really until 1993. But later on, later on as far as the hand-over of weapons is concerned, that improved greatly after 1993 because they realised how well we were working to preserve peace and stability.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that it never required some degree of force to convince reluctant Muslims to share information with the DB?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: What do you mean by "not really"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking not. We did not use force, but I cannot really say because I wasn't at the office all the time that force was never used. It certainly wasn't used with my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: But you acknowledge the possibility that it could have been used without your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: On what basis are you able to accept that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all the propaganda by Natasa Kandic and all the human rights organisations that wrote all kinds of things in huge amounts, things both true and untrue, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In line 21 of the document chart which has now been marked D452, you talk about Muslims going to Turkey for training and then returning to Sandzak. You said: "Some of the trained people returned to Sandzak and we conducted interviews with them to let them know that we knew about them and to gather information about the training and their further intents." Is it really your evidence that these people were happy to share information about their training and further intentions with you with no force being applied?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In his decision ordering Operation May 1993, Jovica Stanisic in two separate places states the need for "energetic measures and actions." In paragraph 34 of your statement, you actually say that: "More energetic measures and actions were required." The reluctance of Muslims in Sandzak to talk to you was one of the reasons that such energetic measures and actions were required; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should not misunderstand energetic measures and actions because I see what you are driving at. We intensified operative work, that means contacts with all people who could be of assistance to us, but in conspiracy. Work that involved the entire operative and technical staff. I see what you are driving at, but you shouldn't be doing that. Energetic measures and actions means intensifying operative work for the purpose of gathering information.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And what does intensifying operative work mean?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intensifying operative work means that there are no longer any working hours, that we work day and night, national holidays, all holidays with the limited resources that we have using our own cars, allocating all the resources that we had to make a work-plan that would be much more intensive in operative terms than before.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And informational interviews or conversations were obviously a part of that work; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we found out that somebody had a rifle, we would invite that person for an informational interview, we would have a discussion with them, and they would more often than not surrender the weapon. We never took anyone in for an interview without reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 of your statement, you say that at the time you were head of the Novi Pazar DB department, you were also carrying out operative activities at the same time. Did those operative activities include you personally conducting informational interviews or conversations?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And would those sometimes take place at the Novi Pazar SUP building?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes, but mostly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: What about at the Novi Pazar police station?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the same thing. We worked at the police station of Novi Pazar, that's the same building where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 of your statement you indicate that the Novi Pazar DB department had seven employees of which five were operative workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, private session, please. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And can we please have 62 [sic] number 6276 on the screen. This is a report of the Humanitarian Law Fund dated 23 March 1994. It's title is: "Police Repression in Sandzak (October 1993 to March 1994)." Unfortunately we don't have a B/C/S translation available yet. Can we please have the top of page 6 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, we don't have a version of this document in Serbian at the moment. I'm going to read a quote and then ask you for a comment. Under the heading 2, the Pester Case, the document says: "According to the Fund's records, more than 300 Muslims were mistreated in police stations in Sjenica, Tutin, and Novi Pazar during November and December 1993. About 20 people from the village of Rasno alone were beaten because they denied possessing weapons. People to whom the Fund spoke alleged that the drives to confiscate weapons, or to force people to obtain and then surrender automatic and semi-automatic weapons, were launched or continued during February and March 1994..." The document then goes on to list the villages where this took place. The document continues saying: "The cases researched revealed the main feature of the police action in the Pester plain: The widespread use of force in police stations, especially against people who insisted that they did not own weapons." Sir, were you aware of these allegations?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of these allegations, but I suppose they are against the public security wing. I know nothing about them. Absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we could scroll down to the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: We'll see the beginning of a statement of a man named NK. And if we could then go to the top -- and his allegations in short are that he was beaten particularly on the soles of his feet. If we could then go to the top of the next page. Just the first paragraph. He says that after being beaten he went home, he reported back to the police station after the holiday as he had been required to do, and he says: "I reported in after the holiday, but didn't take them anything. I found Vlado Corbic, Nikola, and Dzemko there. They offered me coffee and apologised for making a mistake. They said they would treat the rifle I had bought as voluntary disarming." Sir, what is your response to that account?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's incredible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document as a Prosecution exhibit for impeachment only.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Same position that we have no objection to the section that's just been put, but the whole document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the whole document is relevant to impeachment or at least larger portions than what has been put. I mean section 2, certainly the entirety of section 2, is relevant to impeachment; section 3 deals with Prijepolje, which is also an area that witness has given evidence about. I agree that the entire thing wouldn't be relevant to impeachment, but we would ask to be permitted to select more than just a portion read to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Jordash, only for impeachment, I think the witness testified that never any complaint was brought against him and that he denies whatever involvement in whatever violent treatment of persons which were or were not detained or in a police station, so there's a general denial of any of these events happening as described. Under those circumstances, if it's just a description of these kind of allegations, wouldn't it be, even if not read to the witness in view of the testimony as given until now, would it not be relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I withdraw the objection. Can I just put on the record that I'll -- perhaps my learned friend would just indicate whether this is the same organisation that is run by Natasa Kandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: To my knowledge it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have matters clear, I would say. The document, there's in translation yet, so therefore it should be marked for identification. I do not hear from the Simatovic Defence any further objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P3033 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked as such. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, the Chamber considers that it is not possible to conclude the testimony of the witness, not today. I take it that Mr. Jordash would have some questions and there are some further perhaps research to be done both by you, perhaps, and by the Defence. Unfortunately where we always try to avoid the witness has to stay over the weekend, I'm afraid that it's unavoidable.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the Chamber's information, I was just on the point of saying that I'm done. I understand that doesn't solve the problem. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That doesn't solve the problem at this moment. Therefore I suggest that we just continue on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I literally have three questions, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, any questions as far as you are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you anticipated my questions about the stamp, so I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I have commitments elsewhere, but six minutes is time for three questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was the army ever employed to deal with the Sandzak problem, problem of Muslim extremism?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you have a view on what the consequences would have been if they had been?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There probably would have been problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Of which kind?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR CORBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims hated the military. The military was deployed, but then they had to withdraw because it was perceived as being there because of the Muslims and that could have been the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for the last issue, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber has no questions for you which means that this concludes your evidence. At the same time, I hereby inform the parties that there are apparently some issues still pending. You've reserved your position, Mr. Farr. Of course, the Chamber now has heard the testimony and has heard a lot of other stories which, to say the least, are rather contradicting about what may have happened in police stations in Novi Pazar. So, therefore, the Chamber will also consider whether we would need further information about what happened there. This, therefore, means Mr. Corbic that this concludes your testimony for the time being, but I could not exclude under all circumstances that we would need further information. I thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe return home again. I'm addressing the parties --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether under the present circumstances an instruction to the witness would be appropriate or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we still have outstanding RFAs to Serbia. We would ask for the instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection against the instruction? Mr. Corbic, in view of the fact that there is a chance that we would need to hear further evidence from you, you are instructed unless you receive a message that this instruction is lifted, you are instructed not to speak with anyone, how difficult that may be, not to speak with anyone about the testimony you've given up to the moment where you receive notice that you are free again to communicate and speak, et cetera, until that moment, no communication. Thank you very much. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to raise one procedural issue with the parties. DST-040, what is at this moment the estimate of time needed with that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two and a half hours. Could I hear from Mr. Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will also need two and a half hours, perhaps even three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's been a long time since I reviewed my notes on that, if I could send an e-mail later today I'd appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll not receive that, but if you would send it to Chamber staff, copied to the representative of the Registry here in court so that this information which is needed not only for scheduling purposes but also for logistical matters that it will be passed on to those who were asking for this information. Any other matter? If not, this Chamber appreciates the efforts the parties have made to could be conclude the testimony of this witness today. We adjourn we resume on Tuesday 18th of October at quarter past 2.00 in this same Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
